---
name: horizon
description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
---

You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.

## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate

Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.

You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
**shared state**, not meetings:

- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
  another team.
- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).

Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
object in `horizon inbox list --json`.

## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)

**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.

The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):

- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
  item's status current with `--status` and its strategy prose current with
  `--summary` / `--summary-file` (there is no `--strategy` flag). It doubles as
  the **project board**:
  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.

## Your session's identity (environment variables)

The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |

## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)

Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:

- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).

## One-shot discipline (important)

This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).

## Pick the highest-value work

Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.

If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
(it returns to the queue).

## Fresh-context checkpoints

The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
checkpoints:

- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
  clean/build result.

Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
terminal `done` claim.

Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.

## Warnings are work

Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
why.

Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
issue rather than repeated no-op calls.

## Do the work (Lean)

For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
configured final build covers the same files.

**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
mathlib — query it:

| You want | Use | Not |
|---|---|---|
| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |

`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
back to grep.

Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.

- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.

## Read the other projects

They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.

## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)

Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
needs no permission.

Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.

## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)

Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).

Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:

- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status (`--status`) and strategy prose
  (`--summary`), not a re-narration of the diff.
- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
  as **memory**.

Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.

## Resuming after an interruption

State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:

- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.

## Final report (your last message)

Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
not by itself a reason to stop.

## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)

There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
`subagents` skill):

- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.

Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

---
name: project-git
description: How git works in an Archon Horizon workspace — one out-of-tree workspace ledger (no per-project repos); read a project's history by pathspec or by a session's commit trailers.
---

Read this before running `git diff`/`git log` on a project.

## The model

- **One out-of-tree workspace ledger.** Archon commits to a single repo whose git
  dir is `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` with the workspace **root** as its
  work tree (driven via `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`). `<root>/.git` is deliberately
  untouched — it is reserved for a user repo. The ledger records one commit per
  completed session: `config.yaml`, the session's scoped project files, and
  `.archon-horizon/` shared state; never the binary git dirs under
  `.archon-horizon/vcs/`, locks, or other volatile internals.
- **There are no per-project repositories.** A project directory has no nested
  `.git/`, and there is no `.archon-horizon/vcs/<project>.git`. A project's
  "history" is simply the workspace ledger filtered to that project's path.
- **You record your own work by committing to the ledger** with plain `git` (see
  below). Commit *early and often* with a semantic, math-first message — the
  commit message + diff is how your progress is read, so make the message say what
  you proved/built. Provenance trailers are added automatically; do not write them.

So a plain `git diff` at the root sees only a user repo (if any), never Archon's.
Drive the out-of-tree workspace ledger explicitly (or use `hgit`).

## Recording your work (committing)

Commits go to the ledger, **not** to `<root>/.git` and **not** via any project
`.git` (there is none). Do **not** `export GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` yourself — that
would redirect `lake` and other tooling. Two equivalent ways to commit:

```bash
# 1) The `hgit` wrapper (on the session env as $HORIZON_GIT) — plain git, ledger-scoped:
"$HORIZON_GIT" add path/to/File.lean
"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
  --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'

# 2) The explicit form (identical effect):
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    add path/to/File.lean
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
    --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
```

Ordinary git: the ledger's index tracks HEAD, so `add` then `commit` records your
files on top of it. Horizon's own commits stage in a private index and never leave
anything staged in your way.

- **Prefer the pathspec commit** — name the paths on the commit itself:
  `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…" --trailer 'Summary=…' -- path/to/File.lean`
  It records exactly those files, ignores whatever else may be staged, and git
  builds its tree from the **current** HEAD — so it cannot silently revert a
  concurrent session's files the way a commit built on a stale index can.
- Add at least one **`Summary` trailer** explaining the important change, not

    19	This is the **P5-uniform** pre-brick of the Wave-4 datum campaign (`informal/w4-datum-worksheet.md`
    20	§2.1, §4 DAT-0a). It is consumed by DAT-D's uniform Grassmannian twist, where the twist exponent
    21	`M` is chosen so that `deg (Θ^M) ≥ b` and the whole degree-`g` family lands in the vanishing
    22	locus.
    23	
    24	## The route (worksheet §4 DAT-0a, collapsed form)
    25	
    26	The proof is the FLV-class argument (`RiemannRoch/FLVClass.lean`) with the twist specialized to the
    27	fiber divisor `F = fiberWeilDivisor π` and the base twist fixed at the FLV-fiber threshold `n₁` of
    28	`D₀ = 0`:
    29	
    30	* FLV-fiber at `D₀ = 0` (`subsingleton_hModule_divisorSheaf_one_of_isFinite_toP1`) gives `n₁` with
    31	  `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n·F))` for all `n ≥ n₁`; take `n = n₁`, so the base twist `n₁·F` is fixed;
    32	* `0 < deg F` (`zero_lt_deg_fiberWeilDivisor`) makes `b := n₁·deg F + 1 − χ(𝒪_Y)` a legal
    33	  threshold: for `deg D ≥ b` the residual class `[D]·[F]^{-n₁}` has degree `≥ 1 − χ`, so
    34	  `exists_effective_of_picClass` yields an **effective** witness `E` of that class;
    35	* `n₁·F + E` is in the class of `D`; `peel_effective` transports `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n₁·F))` to
    36	  `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n₁·F + E))`, and witness-independence
    37	  (`subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq`, W6-lite) upgrades it to `𝒪(D)`.
    38	
    39	Because `n₁` (hence the base twist) is fixed, the effective witness carries the whole degree slack,
    40	and `b` depends only on `(Y, π)` — exactly the shape DAT-D consumes.
    41	-/
    42	
    43	set_option autoImplicit false
    44	
    45	universe u
    46	
    47	open CategoryTheory Limits Opposite
    48	
    49	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
    50	
    51	open Scheme
    52	
    53	section Uniform
    54	
    55	variable {K : Type u} [Field K] {Y : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral Y]
    56	  [Y.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    57	  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    58	  [LocallyOfFiniteType (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    59	  [QuasiCompact (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
    60	
    61	/-- **DAT-0a — the P5-uniform `H¹`-vanishing bound.** For a **finite** dominant `π : Y ⟶ ℙ¹`
    62	compatible with the structure morphisms, there is a single threshold `b : ℤ`, depending only on
    63	`(Y, π)`, past which the degree-one cohomology of `𝒪(D)` vanishes for **every** Weil divisor `D` of
    64	degree `≥ b`:
    65	
    66	`∃ b, ∀ D, b ≤ deg D → Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(D))`.
    67	
    68	The bound is `b = n₁·deg F + 1 − χ(𝒪_Y)`, with `F = fiberWeilDivisor π` and `n₁` the FLV-fiber
    69	threshold at `D₀ = 0`; see the module docstring for the collapsed route
    70	(`informal/w4-datum-worksheet.md` §4 DAT-0a). Consumed by DAT-D's uniform Grassmannian twist. -/
    71	theorem exists_bound_subsingleton_hModule_one_of_isFinite_toP1
    72	    [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
    73	    [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 1)]
    74	    (π : Y ⟶ P1 K) [IsFinite π] [IsDominant π]
    75	    (hπ : π ≫ P1.structureMap K = Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K)) :
    76	    ∃ b : ℤ, ∀ D : Y.CurveDivisor, b ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K D →
    77	      Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K D) 1) := by
    78	  obtain ⟨n₁, hn₁⟩ :=
    79	    subsingleton_hModule_divisorSheaf_one_of_isFinite_toP1 π hπ (0 : Y.CurveDivisor)
    80	  have hd'pos : 0 < CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) :=
    81	    zero_lt_deg_fiberWeilDivisor π
    82	  refine ⟨(n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) + 1
    83	      - Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K), fun D hD => ?_⟩
    84	  -- the residual class `[D] · [F]^{-n₁}`
    85	  set c : Y.CechPic := CurveDivisor.picClass K D
    86	    * (CurveDivisor.picClass K (fiberWeilDivisor π) ^ n₁)⁻¹ with hc
    87	  have hcdeg : classDeg K c
    88	      = CurveDivisor.deg K D - (n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) := by
    89	    rw [hc, classDeg_mul, classDeg_inv, classDeg_pow, classDeg_picClass, classDeg_picClass]
    90	    ring
    91	  -- an effective witness of the residual class
    92	  obtain ⟨W, hWc⟩ := CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K c
    93	  have hWdeg : 1 ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K W + Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K) := by
    94	    have hWeq : CurveDivisor.deg K W
    95	        = CurveDivisor.deg K D - (n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) := by
    96	      rw [← hcdeg, ← hWc, classDeg_picClass]
    97	    linarith
    98	  obtain ⟨E, hEnonneg, hEc⟩ := exists_effective_of_picClass W hWdeg
    99	  -- the witness divisor `n₁ • F + E` is in the class of `D`
   100	  have hclass : CurveDivisor.picClass K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π + E)
   101	      = CurveDivisor.picClass K D := by
   102	    rw [CurveDivisor.picClass_add, picClass_nsmul, hEc, hWc, hc,
   103	      mul_comm (CurveDivisor.picClass K D), ← mul_assoc, mul_inv_cancel, one_mul]
   104	  -- base vanishing at `n₁ • F`, peel `E`, transport along the class
   105	  have hbase : Subsingleton
   106	      (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π)) 1) := by
   107	    have h := hn₁ n₁ le_rfl
   108	    rwa [zero_add] at h
   109	  have hpeel : Subsingleton
   110	      (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π + E)) 1) :=
   111	    peel_effective (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π) E hEnonneg hbase
   112	  exact subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq K hclass hpeel
   113	
   114	end Uniform
   115	
   116	end AlgebraicGeometry

1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status current with `--status` and its strategy prose current with
60	  `--summary` / `--summary-file` (there is no `--strategy` flag). It doubles as
61	  the **project board**:
62	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
63	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
64	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
65	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
66	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
67	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
68	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
69	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
70	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
71	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
72	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
73	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
74	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
75	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
76	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
77	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
78	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
79	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
80	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
81	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
82	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
83	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
84	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
85	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
86	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
87	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
88	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
89	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
90	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
91	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
92	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
93	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
94	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
95	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
96	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
97	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
98	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
99	
100	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
101	
102	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
103	
104	| Variable | Meaning |
105	|---|---|
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
112	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
113	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
114	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
115	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
116	
117	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
118	
119	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
120	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
121	
122	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
123	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
124	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
125	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
126	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
127	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
128	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
129	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
130	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
131	
132	## One-shot discipline (important)
133	
134	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
135	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
136	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
137	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
138	
139	## Pick the highest-value work
140	
141	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
142	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
143	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
144	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
145	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
146	
147	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
148	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
149	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
150	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
151	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
152	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
153	(it returns to the queue).
154	
155	## Fresh-context checkpoints
156	
157	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
158	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
159	checkpoints:
160	
161	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
162	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
163	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
164	  clean/build result.
165	
166	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
167	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
168	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
169	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
170	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
171	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
172	terminal `done` claim.
173	
174	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
175	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
176	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
177	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
178	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
179	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
180	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
181	
182	## Warnings are work
183	
184	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
185	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
186	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
187	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
188	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
189	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
190	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
191	why.
192	
193	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
194	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
195	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
196	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
197	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
198	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
199	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
200	
201	## Do the work (Lean)
202	
203	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
204	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
205	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
206	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
207	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
208	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
209	configured final build covers the same files.
210	
211	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
212	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
213	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
214	mathlib — query it:
215	
216	| You want | Use | Not |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
219	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
220	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
221	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
222	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
223	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
224	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
225	
226	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
227	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
228	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
229	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
230	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
231	back to grep.
232	
233	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
234	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
235	
236	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
237	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
238	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
239	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
240	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
241	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
242	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
243	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
244	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
245	
246	## Read the other projects
247	
248	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
249	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
250	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
251	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
252	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
253	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
254	
255	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
256	
257	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
258	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
259	needs no permission.
260	
261	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
262	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
263	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
264	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
265	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
266	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
267	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
268	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
269	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
270	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
271	
272	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
273	
274	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
275	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
276	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
277	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
278	
279	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
280	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
281	
282	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status (`--status`) and strategy prose
283	  (`--summary`), not a re-narration of the diff.
284	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
285	  as **memory**.
286	
287	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
288	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
289	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
290	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
291	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
292	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
293	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
294	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
295	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
296	
297	## Resuming after an interruption
298	
299	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
300	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
301	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
302	
303	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
304	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
305	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
306	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
307	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
308	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
309	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
310	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
311	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
312	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
313	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
314	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
315	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
316	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
317	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
318	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
319	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
320	
321	## Final report (your last message)
322	
323	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
324	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
325	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
326	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
327	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
328	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
329	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
330	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
331	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
332	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
333	not by itself a reason to stop.
334	
335	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
336	
337	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
338	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
339	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
340	`subagents` skill):
341	
342	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
343	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
344	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
345	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
346	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
347	
348	Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

---
name: prescriptions-need-auditing-like-measurements
description: A docstring naming "the two bricks this needs" is a claim about proof shape, and nothing audits it the way measurements get audited
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

A docstring that prescribes what a gap *needs* ("without X and Y, no amount of
re-firing produces one") is as load-bearing as one that measures what a gap *is*
— but only measurements get re-checked. The prescription silently sets the price
of the whole residue for every later round.

Measured in AJC `RiemannRoch/Ledger/FiberBound.lean` (run 0074 r7): it named two
bricks for the uniform-base-divisor input. One landed. The other — a Weil divisor
pullback along `C_κ ⟶ C`, priced hard because closed points split — **was never
needed**. The route that worked transported the *vanishing statement* by faithful
flatness and never transported a divisor at all, so it never met the splitting
problem. The uniform bound was the zero divisor, not the prescribed `b(k)`.

**Why:** a residue recorded as "these two bricks" was really one brick plus one
dispensable assumption about the shape of the proof, and the dispensable half is
what made the input look expensive for several rounds. Lanes re-read the
prescription as the cost and never re-derived it.

**How to apply:** when a docstring or handoff says a gap needs specific bricks,
treat the *list* as a hypothesis about proof shape, not a fact. Before pricing
work against it, ask whether a different route avoids the named obstacle
entirely — especially when the obstacle is about transporting an *object*
(divisors, points, covers) and the goal is only to transport a *property*
(vanishing, subsingleton, finiteness). Transporting the statement is often free
where transporting the object is hard. Related: [[absence-claims-need-the-whole-project]],
[[price-the-consumer-carrier]], [[subsingleton-not-finrank-for-vanishing]].

3	description: Read and act on the Archon Horizon inbox — list/filter items, understand labels/kinds, comment, archive, create; per-team ownership and read-state; and message other projects or teams via the `horizon inbox` CLI.
4	---
5	
6	The inbox is the durable channel between the human, agent sessions (present and
7	future), and other projects. Act on it through the CLI; never edit inbox files
8	by hand. Prefer `--json` whenever reading command output for exact ids or
9	fields.
10	
11	## Read
12	
13	- `horizon inbox list` — read the inbox. Use `--json` when you need exact ids,
14	  labels, scope, author, audience, timestamps, or comments. Use the list filters
15	  to narrow without losing the overview: `--to horizon`, `--to human`,
16	  `--project P`, repeated `--kind K`, repeated `--label L`,
17	  `--status open`, `--query TEXT`, `--limit N`, and `--comments N`.
18	- In an agent session, an unqualified list means the **open working queue**, not
19	  archived history. It is ordered by attention: required protections first,
20	  unread/direct conversations next, then advisory items. JSON starts with an
21	  `attention` summary so redirecting stderr cannot erase this signal.
22	- `horizon inbox show <id> --json` opens exactly one item and marks it read for
23	  your team. Use `--no-mark-read` for inspection without acknowledgement.
24	- Every inbox command evaluates the full local working set, even when `list` is
25	  filtered. Treat its advisory warnings as a prompt to review duplicates, stale
26	  memories, and consumed notices. The CLI never archives automatically because
27	  only the working agent can decide what is resolved; that agent must make an
28	  explicit cleanup pass before its final report.
29	- Labels are the release gate. Local inbox items default to `agent-ready`, which
30	  means they are visible to agents at run boundaries. Keep that default for
31	  machine-addressed work, and usually keep it for human-addressed notices too:
32	  it helps later agents see that the human has already been notified and avoids
33	  duplicate reports. Use `not-ready`, `rejected`, or no labels only when there is
34	  a concrete reason agents should not see or act on the item yet.
35	- Audience says who should read the item: empty/general, `horizon`, `human`,
36	  `project:<name>`, or a **direct message** to another team: `task:<id>` /
37	  `run:<id>` (older items may carry the legacy `ground` audience). A conversation
38	  may have several recipients; start one with `horizon inbox dm <recipient>...`.
39	  Scope/project says what the item is about.
40	- Horizon reads general items, items addressed to `horizon`, items addressed
41	  to its project, and DMs addressed to its own task/run. It should ignore other
42	  projects' and other teams' addressed items.
43	- A conversation's participants are its recipients **and its initiator**. The
44	  initiator is recorded as `metadata.started_by`; replies become unread for every
45	  other participant, including that initiator. Participants are not ownership:
46	  the initiator remains responsible for deciding when the thread is finished.
47	- Kinds: `conversation` (a direct/group thread requiring prompt acknowledgement),
48	  `hint` (normal guidance), `issue` (problem to fix/report),
49	  `protection` (standing constraint / soft freeze), `info` (a notice for the
50	  human — something you did or noticed they should know, e.g. a renamed project
51	  or an important change; purely informational, never affects what runs),
52	  `memory` (durable agent note or dead end).
53	
54	## Ownership & read-state (your team's inbox)
55	
56	Each running session is a **team**, and the inbox is shared across teams. Two
57	lightweight overlays keep it navigable:
58	
59	- **Ownership** — an item is either *shared with everyone* (the default) or
60	  *owned by one task* (that team's private inbox — e.g. its own memory). Read your
61	  team's inbox with `horizon inbox list --mine` (owned-by-you **plus** shared);
62	  another team's private items don't appear. Own an item to your task with
63	  `horizon inbox add --mine …` (or `--owner <task-id>`), and `horizon inbox own
64	  <id> --mine|--owner <task>|--shared` to move an existing one. Owning your
65	  `--kind memory` notes keeps another team's memory out of your working set.
66	- **Read-state** — read/unread is **per team**, so a shared item several teams see
67	  tracks who has read it. `horizon inbox list --unread` is what *you* have not read
68	  yet; `horizon inbox read <id>` marks it read, and `horizon inbox unread <id>`
69	  puts it back (e.g. you read it but it still needs action). Combine:
70	  `horizon inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue — the same signal
71	  the pre-command synchronizer counts for you.
72	
73	Read in this order before editing:
74	
75	1. `horizon inbox list --mine --status open --kind protection --json` — every
76	   active protection is required even if your team previously marked it read.
77	2. `horizon inbox list --mine --unread --kind conversation --json` — open each
78	   result with `inbox show`; reply when a response is needed, otherwise the read
79	   acknowledgement clears it until another participant replies.
80	3. Consult hint/issue/info/memory items as advisory context for the task.
81	
82	The reader/owner id is inferred from your session (your task), so you rarely pass
83	it explicitly.
84	
85	## Act
86	
87	Authorship is automatic: every item and comment you create through the CLI is
88	attributed to your role (normally `horizon`) from the run environment — you do
89	**not** pass `--author` (a stray `--author work-reviewer` is demoted to the
90	`agent` metadata, not used as the author, so the author set stays conventional).
91	If you are a dispatched **subagent**, add `--agent <your-name>` (e.g. `--agent
92	work-reviewer`) to record your identity; it is stored in metadata and shown
93	next to the role in the UI, keeping the author itself a clean role. Items and
94	comments are also auto-tagged with the run/session provenance (a small chip in the
95	UI); you do not pass this yourself.
96	
97	New inbox items use a two-part body:
98	
99	- First paragraph = concise title. Keep it short enough to scan in one UI row
100	  (aim for under ~100 characters); do not put the full explanation here.
101	- Second paragraph and later = non-empty description. Put the evidence, impact,
102	  next action, and relevant ids/files here. The description is **mandatory** — an
103	  item that is only a title is rejected.
104	
105	Write bodies and comments in **Markdown**: the dashboard renders it. Use short
106	paragraphs and `-` bullet lists instead of one wall-of-text paragraph, `**bold**`
107	for the key claim, and backticks for ids, lemma names, files, and code
108	(`` `lem:foo` ``, `` `Foo.lean:42` ``). For a multi-part result, start with a
109	one-sentence conclusion, then use `## Result`, `## Evidence`, `## Impact`, and
110	`## Next action` as applicable; omit empty sections. The CLI rejects long new
111	agent descriptions, opening messages, and comments with no paragraph, heading,
112	or list structure.
113	
114	Do not create an item whose body is only a title. If you need a `[persistent]` or
115	`[temporary]` tag, put it at the start of the title paragraph and keep the rest
116	of that paragraph concise.

124	obvious and then run `horizon inbox archive <id>`.

126	### Conversation lifecycle
127	
128	A conversation is for an expected reply, decision, or active coordination. A
129	one-way handoff or announcement is an `info`/`hint`, not a conversation.

136	   final decision as comments on that thread. Start another only when it has a
137	   genuinely different decision boundary or participant set.
138	3. **Answer before branching:** when a conversation becomes unread, open it and
139	   answer or acknowledge it before starting another conversation with the same
140	   team.
141	4. **The initiator closes:** if `metadata.started_by` is your task/run, you own
142	   the lifecycle. Once the requested answer has arrived and been consumed, add a
143	   short conclusion comment when the outcome is not obvious, then
144	   `horizon inbox archive <id>`. Do this during the session, not only after a
145	   warning says the inbox is full.
146	5. **Do not hide an answer from its initiator:** recipients normally reply and
147	   leave closure to the initiator. For a human-started thread, answer it but leave
148	   it open for the human to consume/archive unless the human explicitly delegates
149	   closure. Use `complete` instead of `archive` only when the concluded thread is
150	   intentionally meant to remain visible in the resolved working record.
151	6. **End-of-session sweep:** before the final report, inspect open conversations
152	   in which your task is `started_by`. Archive every resolved one and state a real
153	   blocker on any that must remain open. An accumulation of open conversations is
154	   unfinished coordination, not harmless history.
155	
156	- `horizon inbox comment <id> --body "..."` — progress note on an item (record
157	  what you did; not to ask the human for clarification). Do not write your name
158	  into the comment body; the author is set automatically. Drop a comment at each **key advance**
159	  while you work an item (a milestone reached, a route ruled out, a blocker hit),
160	  not only at the end — these comments are the item's visible progress trail.
161	- `horizon inbox dm task:<id> [task:<id> ...] --body "Topic\n\nOpening message"`
162	  — start a one-to-one or group conversation. Use `horizon ps` to discover live
163	  teams. Use it only after the lifecycle search above. The sender remains a
164	  participant and owns closure; every reply makes the thread unread for the other
165	  participants. Humans read and reply from the live dashboard.
166	- **Write comments as mathematics, for a human.** State the key step that
167	  succeeded in human-readable mathematical language (LaTeX for formulas), naming
168	  the result and the idea — e.g. "Proved $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})=0$ for $i>\dim X$ by
169	  reducing to the affine case via Čech cohomology." Mention Lean declaration
170	  names and file paths only as supporting detail; the substance is the maths, not
171	  a code changelog. This applies to comments on **roadmap items and tasks** too:
172	  when a key step lands, record it there in the same mathematical, legible style.
173	- `horizon inbox archive <id>` — soft-delete: keep the item for the record but
174	  hide it from the dashboard by default. Use for stale, superseded, consumed, or
175	  no-longer-key context. Keeping the inbox tidy this way is your job (or the
176	  janitor subagent's) — prune memory/info so they remain small.
177	  For a conversation you initiated, this is the normal "discussion finished"
178	  operation after its answer/conclusion has been consumed.
179	- `horizon inbox complete <id>` — mark an item resolved only when it records work
180	  you genuinely concluded and want to keep visible outside the archive. Before
181	  completing, add a short **conclusion comment**: first the mathematical
182	  conclusion (what was proved/established, in words + LaTeX), then concise
183	  metadata (runs, approximate LOC, files/declarations involved). A reader should
184	  grasp the result and how it was concluded without opening the logs.
185	- `horizon inbox add --body "Short title\n\nDescription with details and next action." [--to R] [--project P] [--persistent|--temporary] [--agent <name> if a subagent]`
186	  — open a new item.
187	  - `--to` is the recipient: `horizon`, `human`, `project:<name>`, or a direct
188	    message to another team `task:<id>` / `run:<id>`.
189	    Use `--to project:<name>` to message another project (e.g. "I rewrote your
190	    `foo` declaration more cleanly, you may want it"); use `--to task:<id>` to
191	    message a specific running team.
192	  - `--owner <task-id>` / `--mine` keeps the item in one team's inbox instead of
193	    the shared default.
194	  - `--project` says what the item is ABOUT (its subject).
195	  - `--persistent` / `--temporary` just prepend a `[persistent]` / `[temporary]`
196	    tag to the body.
197	  - `--pending` labels the item `not-ready` instead of the default `agent-ready`,
198	    so it stays invisible to agents until a human releases it.
199	- `horizon inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body "Short memory title\n\nDurable fact, convention, or dead end."` — record a durable
200	  note / dead end. Memory lives in the inbox, so it is rendered in the "Memory"
201	  section and a human can prune it like any other item.
202	- `horizon inbox protect --body "..." [--project P] [--file F] [--declaration D] [--blueprint-node N]`
203	  — add a semantic standing constraint the Horizon agent must respect (a soft freeze),
204	  e.g. "do not change the signature of `Foo.bar`". These render as a
205	  "Protected" section; honour them, including semantic ones. For a target that
206	  must be mechanically blocked before dispatch, the user uses the config-backed
207	  `horizon freeze add <file|declaration|blueprint-node> <target>` command instead.
208	
209	Reading convention: an item tagged `[persistent]` is a standing rule — respect
210	it every round and keep it open while relevant. `[temporary]` (or untagged) is
211	one-shot — archive it once consumed. Items in the "Protected" section are never
212	modified.

`Ledger/ExtensionUniformity.uniformVanishing_of_uniform_base_of_genus_invariant` needed two

cluster-P statements have been conflated before:

* What changed is the *size of the residue*, not its status: extension-uniformity was two open
  inputs, and is now exactly one, named, with no genus hypothesis anywhere in the statement.
* Nothing here touches global generation, and nothing here makes generation uniform over
  extensions.  That remains a single-field statement (`FiberBound`, item 3). -/

section Reduction

variable {k : Type u} [Field k] (C : Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)))

/-- **Non-vacuity: the cover argument is not a hidden hypothesis.**  `genus_baseChangeField` and
the reduction below take an `AffineCoverMVSquare` on `C.left`, and a statement taking a datum the
project cannot produce would be vacuous progress.  It can: on AJC's curve a 2-affine cover
follows from the three curve binders alone, via `Ledger/MapToP1`'s finite dominant `π : C ⟶ ℙ¹`
pulled back along the standard ℙ¹ charts (`Adelic.P1HasLaurentChartData` is a global instance
over every field, `Adelic.LaurentChartData.pullbackSquare` does the pullback).

Stated as a theorem rather than asserted in a docstring, because "the caller supplies a cover"
and "no caller can" look identical from the statement. -/
theorem nonempty_affineCoverMVSquare_of_curve [IsProper C.hom]
    [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] :
    Nonempty C.left.AffineCoverMVSquare := by
  obtain ⟨S, -⟩ := Adelic.exists_affineCoverMVSquare_module_finite_H1Cok C
  exact ⟨S⟩

/-- **The genus identity with the cover discharged** (★★): `genus C_κ = genus C` for every field
extension, on the three curve binders and **nothing else** — no cover argument.

This is the form a downstream consumer should call.  It is `genus_baseChangeField` composed with
`nonempty_affineCoverMVSquare_of_curve`, and the composition is what makes "for every field
extension" an unqualified claim about AJC's curve rather than one about curves that happen to
come with a cover. -/
theorem genus_baseChangeField_curve [IsProper C.hom] [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom] [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom]
    (κ : Type u) [Field κ] [Algebra k κ] :
    genus (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ) = genus C := by
  obtain ⟨S⟩ := nonempty_affineCoverMVSquare_of_curve C
  exact Scheme.genus_baseChangeField κ S

/-- **The reduction with the cover discharged too** (★★): extension-uniform bounded vanishing
follows from `UniformBaseDivisor C d` alone, on the three curve binders.

`UniformBaseDivisor C d` is the **one** remaining open input.  Nothing else is assumed.

**The shape of that gap, measured rather than described.**  Applying the producer/consumer test
of I-0711 (from the AJCR certificate lane, which spent three sessions mis-pricing exactly this):
ask whether a declaration exists whose *conclusion* is the type in question, with primitive
inputs.  For every comparison in this file and its companion, one does — `sectionsBaseChangeField`
from a qcqs open, `h1CokₗBaseChangeField` from a cover, `nonempty_affineCoverMVSquare_of_curve`
from the three curve binders.  For `UniformBaseDivisor` **none does**: it is a `def` with five
consumers and no producer anywhere in AJC.

So the gap is not a missing consumer or a carrier mismatch — it is a missing **production from
geometry**, and that is the form the next attempt should take.

**That measurement has since been acted on, and its "no producer" clause is now false as
stated.**  `Ledger/VanishingFieldDescent.uniformBaseDivisor_zero_of_subsingleton` is a producer:
its conclusion is `UniformBaseDivisor C 0` and its input is a property of `C` alone.  The
prediction the paragraph made was right about the *form* — it came from geometry, via faithfully
flat descent of the `H¹` comparison this file builds — and wrong about the *difficulty*, since it

hypothesis `Subsingleton (H¹(𝒪_C))` is `genus C = 0`, so `genus C ≥ 1` is untouched and the
sentence above still describes that case correctly. -/
theorem uniformVanishing_of_uniformBaseDivisor_curve [IsProper C.hom]
    [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] {d : ℤ} (hbase : UniformBaseDivisor C d) :
    UniformVanishing C :=
  uniformVanishing_of_uniform_base_of_genus_invariant C (g := genus C) hbase
    (fun κ _ _ => genus_baseChangeField_curve C κ)

/-- **Extension-uniform bounded vanishing from the base-divisor bound alone** (★★): with base-field
invariance of the genus now a theorem (§3), the reduction of `Ledger/ExtensionUniformity.lean`
carries only its second antecedent.

`UniformBaseDivisor C d` — one degree bound `d` such that over *every* extension `κ/k` some
divisor of degree `≤ d` already has vanishing `H¹` — is **the single remaining gap** in
extension-uniformity, and it is open in AJC and in AJCR both.  The threshold produced here is
`d + genus C`, an honest constant of `C` with no `κ` in it.

The cover argument is supplied by the caller, since `genus_baseChangeField` reads the genus on
one; on the challenge curve `Adelic.LaurentChartData.pullbackSquare` produces it. -/
theorem uniformVanishing_of_uniformBaseDivisor [IsProper C.hom]
    [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
    [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] (S : C.left.AffineCoverMVSquare) {d : ℤ}
    (hbase : UniformBaseDivisor C d) :
    UniformVanishing C :=
  uniformVanishing_of_uniform_base_of_genus_invariant C (g := genus C) hbase
    (fun κ _ _ => Scheme.genus_baseChangeField κ S)

end Reduction

    10	
    11	Measured **at synthesis sites**, not at the declarations.  The distinction is the whole point of
    12	this file and it is the specific error the task warned about: a theorem quantifying over a gate
    13	instance reports clean axioms *as stated* and only picks up `sorryAx` where the instance is

    19	## Controls
    20	
    21	Two negative controls are included and **must** report `sorryAx`.  Without them a clean reading
    22	proves nothing — a probe that tests names that do not exist, or that measures a statement whose
    23	instances were never forced, reads clean for the wrong reason.  (This lane shipped phantom
    24	declaration names three times; the controls are the guard against a fourth.)

    27	set_option autoImplicit false

    39	variable [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom] [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom]
    40	variable (κ : Type u) [Field κ] [Algebra k κ]

    44	/-- Synthesis site: the field extension is faithfully flat. -/

    46	  Scheme.faithfullyFlat_of_field_extension κ

    50	-- NOTE on probe shape: each probe below **returns the statement**, it does not merely `have` it
    51	-- and close with `trivial`.  A `True`-valued probe that discards the term does not retain its
    52	-- axiom dependencies, so `#print axioms` on it measures nothing.  (Caught in this very file: an
    53	-- earlier draft used the `have _ := …; trivial` shape and three probes then read `sorryAx` from a
    54	-- syntax error elsewhere in the script rather than from the theorems — the controls are what
    55	-- exposed it.)
    56	
    57	omit [IsProper C.hom] [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
    58	  [GeometricallyIntegral C.hom] in
    59	/-- Synthesis site: the Čech-carrier equivalence, at a produced cover.  The `omit` is informative:
    60	§2's Čech-level equivalence genuinely needs **no** curve hypothesis — only the cover — which is
    61	what makes it the faithful-flatness statement rather than a geometric one. -/

    65	      Subsingleton (S.H1Cokₗ C (SheafOfModules.unit C.left.ringCatSheaf)) :=
    66	  Scheme.subsingleton_h1Cokₗ_unit_baseChangeField_iff κ S
    67	
    68	omit [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom] in
    69	/-- Synthesis site: the `Sheaf.HModule`-carrier equivalence, at a produced cover.  Geometric
    70	irreducibility is not needed once a cover is supplied — it is `nonempty_affineCoverMVSquare_of_curve`

    73	    letI : C.left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) := .ofHom C.hom
    74	    letI : (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of κ)) :=
    75	      .ofHom (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).hom
    76	    Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule ((Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).left.moduleKSheaf κ) 1) ↔
    77	      Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1) :=
    78	  Scheme.subsingleton_hModule_one_moduleKSheaf_baseChangeField_iff κ S
    79	
    80	/-- Synthesis site: the cover-discharged form.  This is the one that matters — it binds only the
    81	three curve hypotheses, so the whole `AffineCoverMVSquare` production runs here. -/
    82	theorem probeIffCurve :
    83	    letI : C.left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) := .ofHom C.hom
    84	    letI : (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of κ)) :=
    85	      .ofHom (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).hom
    86	    Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule ((Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).left.moduleKSheaf κ) 1) ↔
    87	      Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1) :=
    88	  subsingleton_hModule_one_baseChangeField_iff_curve C κ
    89	
    90	/-! ### §3 the producer and the `UniformVanishing` instance -/
    91	
    92	/-- Synthesis site: the producer for `UniformBaseDivisor`. -/
    93	theorem probeProducer
    94	    (h : letI : C.left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) := .ofHom C.hom
    95	         Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1)) :
    96	    UniformBaseDivisor C 0 :=
    97	  uniformBaseDivisor_zero_of_subsingleton C h
    98	
    99	/-- Synthesis site: the first `UniformVanishing` instance. -/
   100	theorem probeUniformVanishing
   101	    (h : letI : C.left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) := .ofHom C.hom
   102	         Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1)) :
   103	    UniformVanishing C :=
   104	  uniformVanishing_of_subsingleton_h1 C h
   105	
   106	/-! ### Negative controls -/
   107	
   108	/-- **Control 1** — must report `sorryAx`.  Guards against a probe that reads clean because it
   109	measured nothing.  Stated in the *same shape* as the real probes (returns its statement) so it
   110	tests the same measurement path they use. -/
   111	theorem probeControlOne :
   112	    letI : C.left.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) := .ofHom C.hom
   113	    Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1) := sorry
   114	
   115	/-- **Control 2** — must report `sorryAx`.  A control living in the *same* section, under the same
   116	binders, so it also confirms the binder block itself is not what launders the reading. -/
   117	theorem probeControlTwo : UniformBaseDivisor C 37 := sorry

   124	#print axioms probeH1CokIff
   125	#print axioms probeHModuleIff
   126	#print axioms probeIffCurve

   128	#print axioms probeUniformVanishing

   132	#print axioms AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.h1CokₗBaseChangeField

   136	#print axioms AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.divisorSheafZeroIso

   141	#print axioms probeControlOne
   142	#print axioms probeControlTwo
